name: Bent-over row
joint: Shoulder, elbow, hip, knee and ankle
angleNote: Pull: 0% = arms hanging straight, 100% = load at the trunk. The trunk angle is held by the variant. Hip, knee and ankle torques are per leg; shoulder and elbow per arm.

strength.note: Relative isometric hip-extension torque vs hip flexion, peak about 53°, measured standing with the knee slightly bent (tested −29° to 74°; deeper hip flexion is held flat at the 74° value, which is extrapolation). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Relative isometric knee-extension torque vs knee flexion: weakest near full extension, peak about 65° (Anderson, tested 0–103°). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Lindahl et al. found the same shape (peak near 50°, about 50% of peak at 10°). Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022; Lindahl O, Movin A, Ringqvist I (1969/1972). Isometric knee extension strength as a function of joint angle, muscle length and motor unit activity. Acta Orthop Scand 43:138–147

strength.note: Relative isometric plantarflexion torque vs plantarflexion (negative = dorsiflexed), peak about 23° of dorsiflexion, measured with the knee bent 50° (tested 29° dorsiflexion to 34° plantarflexion). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Shoulder extension (positive) and flexion (negative) peak torque per arm, taken as constant across the range: Mayer's isometric means for men (93 and 68 Nm), measured standing.
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric)

strength.note: Relative isometric elbow-flexion torque vs elbow flexion (0° = straight), peak about 95°: the paper's mean cubic fit, normalised, inside the measured 32–120° (held flat beyond). Measured with the upper arm raised 90° and horizontally adducted 20°, not hanging as in a standing curl. Peak per arm: the paper's male means (flexion 85 Nm, extension 77 Nm).
strength.source: Pinter IJ, Bobbert MF, van Soest AJ, Smeets JBJ (2010). Isometric torque–angle relationships of the elbow flexors and extensors in the transverse plane. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 20:923–931. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2010.05.001

muscles.name: Latissimus dorsi
muscles.note: Main shoulder extensor: pulls the upper arm back towards the hips.

muscles.name: Posterior deltoid
muscles.note: Extends the shoulder with the lats; also pulls the arm out to the side when the elbows flare (not in this side-view model).

muscles.name: Biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis
muscles.note: Elbow flexors: work while the forearm is tilted away from the line of the load.

muscles.name: Rhomboids, middle trapezius
muscles.note: Pull the shoulder blades together at the top. Not estimated: the model has no shoulder blade.

muscles.name: Erector spinae
muscles.note: Hold the spine straight against the trunk's and the load's weight, isometrically for the whole set. Approximation: driven by the hip's effort.

muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.note: Hold the hip bend (with the glutes) and pull the knee back: the knee torque here is a flexor one, as in the Romanian deadlift.

variants.name: Barbell row, trunk about 45°
variants.notes: Hips bent 60°, knees 20°, bar pulled to the lower ribs. The trunk lean puts a steady load on the hips and lower back while the arms work. The hands move in a straight line from hanging to the trunk; the elbows stay in the side view's plane (tucked), so elbow flare and the shoulder blades aren't modelled.

variants.name: Trunk horizontal (Pendlay-style)
variants.notes: Trunk about horizontal, bar to the lower chest: the longest lever for the hips and lower back, and the most shoulder extension (lats) at the top. Each rep starts from a hang here, not from the floor. The hands move in a straight line from hanging to the trunk; the elbows stay in the side view's plane (tucked), so elbow flare and the shoulder blades aren't modelled.

variants.name: More upright (Yates-style)
variants.notes: Hips bent only 30°, bar to the belly: much less hip and lower-back load. The load moves mostly up along the trunk, so the shoulder does little and the elbow flexors more. The hands move in a straight line from hanging to the trunk; the elbows stay in the side view's plane (tucked), so elbow flare and the shoulder blades aren't modelled.

phases.name: Hang
phases.text: Arms straight: the hips and back hold the load; the arms barely work.

phases.name: Pull
phases.text: Elbows bend and move back: the elbow flexors peak as the forearm tilts.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Load at the trunk: the shoulder extensors (lats) work hardest, and the shoulder blades squeeze together.
